extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, scientific method, and philosophy of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the epistemic status and strength of generalizations (universal and approximate) derived from experience, including distinctions between co-existence and succession, criteria for empirical laws, and how to apply approximate generalizations to particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish co-existence from succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities in the co-existence of properties (e.g., 'all crows are black') differ fundamentally from uniformities in the succession of phenomena (causal sequences); there is no general axiom for co-existence analogous to the law of causation for succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat methods founded on causation (Methods of Agreement/Difference/Concomitant Variations) as applicable to co-existences. Recognize that co-existence uniformities lack an elimination principle and therefore cannot attain the same scientific certainty as causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify properties as ultimate or derivative
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property (e.g., blackness) is an ultimate property of a kind, it is independent of causation; if it varies among individuals of the same kind, it is likely derivative (the effect of causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether the property can vary without change of kind. If variable, treat the generalization as an empirical law grounded in causation; if apparently invariable, still remain open to discovery of new kinds or overlooked variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical scope limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations respecting co-existence are entitled to reception only as empirical laws and should be presumed true only within the limits of the time, place, and circumstances in which observations were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a generalization, always record the observational limits; avoid unqualified universal extension beyond observed contexts unless causal grounds justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure certainty by improbability of unnoticed exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of certainty of a generalization based solely on past observation ('All crows are black') is measured by the improbability that an exception could have existed to date without being observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how likely it is that counterexamples could have escaped detection (e.g., overlooked new kinds, local undiscovered species, or accidental variations). Use this improbability as the basis for credence in the generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two routes for potential counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: If alleged non-conforming instances exist, either (1) the property is accidental/caused and can vary among the same kind, or (2) the non-conforming instances belong to a distinct, previously unrecognized kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between casual variation (implying causal dependence) and discovery of new kinds; each has different implications for how the generalization should be revised or retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality increases evidential strength (when empirical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more general an empirical generalization (covering many kinds or a large proportion of things), the stronger the evidence for it, because it shows stability across many combinations and fewer possible counteracting causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer more general empirical regularities when they have been observed across wide and varied instances, but still temper confidence by considering the possibility of unknown counteracting causes or undiscovered kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: When causation is unknown, examine all sub-kinds before generalizing upward
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal propositions about superior kinds, unless grounded on proved or presumed connection by causation, ought not to be asserted except after separately examining every known sub-kind (infimæ species) included in the larger kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring that a property true for several species will hold for the entire genus without explicit examination of intervening or intermediate species; be ready to abandon such generalizations on encountering anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat uniformities of co-existence as empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of co-existence—whether ultimate or derivative—must be ranked among empirical laws and are amenable to the same rules as unresolved laws depending on causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same sceptical, context-bound reasoning to co-existence uniformities as to other empirical generalizations; do not accord them special metaphysical certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations are distinct and often necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Many important inductive truths are of the form 'Most A are B' rather than universal; these approximate generalizations are central to probable inference and practical decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize their utility for action and prediction despite lower certainty; their role in science is often preparatory—used to identify candidates for more precise laws—but they may be indispensable in moral or rapid practical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations must be treated as empirical and circumscribed
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions like 'Most A are B' cannot be laws of causation and are reliable only within the observed limits of place, time, and circumstance unless we know the causes that underlie them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not extend approximate generalizations beyond their observed domain unless you can justify extension by causal knowledge or corroborating marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal/criterion-based checks to simple averages when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: When an approximate generalization is not the limit of knowledge, and causes or distinguishing marks of B are known, one can verify whether most A are B either by direct frequency or by checking the presence of the cause/mark in the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ancillary knowledge (frequency of causes, presence of marks) to bolster or test approximate generalizations; this indirect mode of confirmation can be preferable when direct enumeration is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply numerical proportions appropriately to individual cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If an empirical law states 'nine out of every ten A are B', then any particular unknown A has one chance in ten of being not-B — but this holds only within observed limits and only for average, uncharacterized instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply genus-level averages to instances known to be of a particular sub-species or under special circumstances. Use averages only when the individual is not known or presumed to deviate from the average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine approximate generalizations carefully (addition vs. deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using two or more approximate generalizations together, (1) if both apply directly to the case, probabilities can combine (Addition) to raise confidence; (2) if one applies only via the other (a chain), the combined probability will be lower (Ratiocination/Deduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish independent supporting premises from chained premises; examples: two independent witnesses (addition) vs. a witness reporting a second witness (deduction), which is weaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting coarse generalizations when narrower, reliable marks exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Although approximate generalizations are sometimes the only practical guide, whenever one can directly recognize a cause or mark that reliably indicates B, the uncertain generalization should be replaced by the certain criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In decisions (e.g., whether to believe a witness), prefer checking individual marks (honesty, interest, accuracy) over relying solely on general 'most people tell the truth' heuristics when those marks are accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized beings are especially likely to have derivative properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Because organisms are highly modifiable and subject to many causes, properties in organized beings (species, individuals) are more likely to be derivative and variable than properties of simple substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially cautious generalizing about living organisms; expect variability and causal dependence, and look for environmental or developmental causes when properties vary among individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remain open to credible exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even widely-confirmed generalizations should be revised in the face of credible eyewitness testimony or evidence of exceptions (e.g., a credible report of a white crow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess credibility of reported exceptions on their merits (circumstances of observation, credibility of witness). Credible exceptions legitimately overthrow empirical generalizations within their scope.
